questions.prompt: For x' = −kx with k > 0, can explicit Euler produce a growing numerical solution?
options: Yes, if h k > 2 the multiplier 1 − hk has magnitude above 1
No, because the exact solution decays, so the numerical one must too
Only if k is negative, since a positive k always damps
Only for nonlinear equations, never for linear ones like this
questions.explanation: The exact equation is stable, the discretisation is not: |1 − hk| < 1 needs 0 < hk < 2.

questions.prompt: To simulate q'' = a(q, v) with a first-order integrator, what is the state?
options: (q, a) with q' = a and a' = v
(v, a) only, with v' = a
q alone, with q' = a
(q, v) with q' = v and v' = a
questions.explanation: Second-order equations become first-order systems by adding the velocity.

questions.prompt: The update q += h*v; v += h*a(q) (with the updated q) is best described as…
options: Backward Euler, which solves an implicit equation at each step
RK4 with a fixed step and four slope stages per step
Semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler: not the same as explicit Euler
Explicit Euler, since it only uses the old state in both updates
questions.explanation: Using the new q in the velocity update changes the method and gives bounded energy for oscillators.

questions.prompt: T' = −k(T − T_room) with k > 0 settles at which value?
options: 0, because T' is proportional to −T for k > 0
T(0), because the temperature stays at its start
The mean of T(0) and T_room, halfway between them
T_room, because T' = 0 there and the deviation decays
questions.explanation: Shift u = T − T_room to get u' = −ku, so u → 0.

questions.prompt: Explicit Euler is applied to x′ = −x, x(0)=1, on [0,1] with h = 0.02. Using the leading term of the global error, e_N ≈ −(h/2)·T·e^(−T), what is |e_N|? Give it multiplied by 1000 (three decimals).
questions.explanation: x_N=(1−h)^N = exp(N ln(1−h)) = exp(−T − Nh²/2 − …) = e^(−T)(1 − hT/2 + O(h²)), so e_N ≈ −(h/2)T e^(−T). With h=0.02, T=1: 0.01×0.367879 = 0.003679, i.e. 3.679 after multiplying by 1000. The error is proportional to h (global first order), unlike the O(h²) local error of one step.

questions.skillLabel: Stability function of an explicit Runge–Kutta method
questions.prompt: Classical RK4 is applied to x′ = −1000x with h = 0.01, so z = hλ = −10. Its amplification per step is R(z)=1+z+z²/2+z³/6+z⁴/24. Compute R(−10) (nearest integer).
questions.explanation: R(−10) = 1 − 10 + 50 − 1000/6 + 10000/24 = 1 − 10 + 50 − 166.667 + 416.667 = 291. Since |R| > 1, the numerical solution of a decaying equation grows about 291 times per step: fourth-order accuracy does not enlarge the stability region (real limit about −2.785).

questions.skillLabel: Choosing an integrator for a stiff system
questions.prompt: A simulation has a fast stable mode (rate 1000 s⁻¹) and slow dynamics of interest, run with h = 0.01 s. Which statement is correct?
options: Backward Euler is stable here (factor 1/11), at some cost in accuracy.
RK4 is stable here because its fourth-order accuracy makes the step error negligible.
Tightening the tolerance of an explicit solver lets h = 0.01 s become stable.
Semi-implicit Euler fixes the instability because it conserves energy for any step size.
questions.explanation: With z = hλ = −10, explicit Euler (|1+z|=9) and RK4 (R=291) are outside their stability regions and blow up whatever their order. Backward Euler has R=1/(1−z)=1/11 and is stable for every h on a decaying mode (A-stability), at the cost of first-order accuracy and some numerical damping, so it is the natural choice (or a stiff solver such as Radau/BDF). Reducing the tolerance does not change the stability limit of an explicit method, and symplectic Euler is for conservative oscillators, not for stiff decay.
